items.body: الاعتذار لن يغير شيئًا بدأ كيليان مبابي مهاجم ريال مدريد، يشعر بالفعل بآثار الجدل الدائر حول الفيديو الذي ظهر فيه مؤخرًا، ووصف فيه ماو تسي تونغ الزعيم الصيني السابق بـ"الديكتاتور". نتيجة لهذا الفيديو، أعرب الحكومة الصينية على الفور عن استيائها الشديد من تصريح مبابي، وقام التلفزيون الرسمي الصيني بتعليق بث مباريات الدوري الإسباني جزئياً، بينما أعلن العديد من الرعاة الصينيين إنهاء شراكاتهم مع المهاجم الفرنسي. وذكرت شبكة " فوت ميركاتو " نقلًا عن صحيفة "ليكيب" الفرنسية، أن هذا الأمر ينطبق على شركة بوشويلا، وهي شركة مشروبات طاقة، والتي استخدم اللاعب صوته وصورته لصالحها، بجانب شركة مينجنيو، وهي شركة ألبان مشهورة في الصين. ويدرّ هذان العقدان على لاعب ريال مدريد حوالي 7 ملايين يورو سنويًا، وكان من المقرر أن ينتهيا في فبراير ومارس 2027 على التوالي، ولولا هذه الضجة، لكان من المرجح جدًا تجديدهما. وأشارت الصحيفة إلى أن اعتذار مبابي لن يغير في الأمر شيئًا. وكان مبابي قد نشر بيان اعتذار أمس قال فيه : "خلال مقابلة أجريت معي مؤخرًا، علّقت على صورة لي، لكن تعليقي لم يكن موفقًا، وأدرك الآن أنه تسبب في إيذاء مشاعر كثيرين في الصين والجاليات الصينية حول العالم". وأضاف: "أعتذر لكل من تسببت كلماتي في إزعاجه، فلم يكن ذلك مقصدي على الإطلاق. أكنّ احترامًا عميقًا للشعب الصيني وتاريخه، وأعرب عن أسفي الصادق". …

items.summary: حجي يتغنى بنجم باريس سان جيرمان ويعتبره قدوة للشباب
items.body: حجي يتغنى بنجم باريس سان جيرمان ويعتبره قدوة للشباب يرى مصطفى حجي، أسطورة المنتخب المغربي، أن أشرف حكيمي، وياسين بونو هما الأفضل في تاريخ أسود الأطلس "بفارق كبير عن باقي الأساطير". ورغم تألق عدد كبير من الأساطير بقميص المنتخب المغربي، فإن حجي يرى أن حكيمي، يليه بونو، يتقدمان بفارق كبير على بقية الأسماء، وفقًا لتقييمه الشخصي. وقال حجي، في حوار مصور لكووورة سينشر لاحقًا ، "نعم، حكيمي هو أفضل لاعب في تاريخ الكرة المغربية بفارق كبير عن أي لاعب آخر، هو بعيد جدًا عن الآخرين". ثم أضاف "حكيمي قدوة للشباب المغربي داخل الملعب، وأرى أنه يأتي في صدارة القائمة، وياسين بونو في المركز الثاني، ثم يأتي البقية بفارق كبير عنهما". وعندما سُئل عن موقعه بين أساطير الكرة المغربية عبر التاريخ، رد حجي ضاحكًا "لا، أنا بعيد عن ذلك". وخاض حكيمي 103 مباريات دولية بقميص المنتخب المغربي في كل البطولات، وهو ثاني أكثر لاعب مشاركة في تاريخ الأسود، إذ لا يتفوق عليه سوى نور الدين نيبت (115 مباراة). ويأتي بونو ثالثًا في هذه القائمة برصيد 99 مباراة. وبعيدًا عن المباريات الدولية، توج حكيمي بجائزة أفضل لاعب في أفريقيا لعام 2025، وينافس بقوة على لقب الجائزة ذاتها في 2026. ويملك حكيمي ألقابًا أوروبية مرموقة مع الأندية التي لعب لها، يأتي على رأسها الفوز بدوري أبطال أوروبا 3 مرات. اقرأ أيضًا: مصطفى حجي لكووورة: المغرب يمكنه…

items.summary: تحفيز للمستقبل
items.body: تحفيز للمستقبل دعم هوجو لوريس، قائد منتخب فرنسا السابق، نجم الديوك وريال مدريد كيليان مبابي، بعد خسارته في سباق الكرة الذهبية. وذهبت الجائزة المرموقة التي تقدمها مجلة فرانس فوتبول إلى قائد منتخب إنجلترا، مهاجم نادي بايرن ميونخ هاري كين، خلال الحفل الذي أقيم في لندن، مساء الإثنين. ناقش الموضوعات والأخبار بشكل أعمق في منتديات كووورة اقرأ أيضا: هل فقدت قصة ميسي تأثيرها؟.. معايير الكرة الذهبية في قفص الاتهام وفي تصريحات لصحيفة "ليكيب" الفرنسية، عبّر حارس مرمى لوس أنجيليس إف سي عن ثقته في قدرة زميله السابق بالمنتخب الفرنسي على الفوز بأرفع الجوائز الفردية في كرة القدم يومًا ما. وقال لوريس: "الظروف لم تكن مواتية بعد، لكن هذا سيجعله أقوى. لديه كل ما يلزم للفوز بها يومًا ما". واحتل مبابي المركز الثاني في تصويت الكرة الذهبية، بينما جاء لامين يامال نجم برشلونة، في المركز الثالث. ونال مبابي جائزة هداف الدوري الإسباني في الموسم الماضي برصيد (25) هدفا، وهداف دوري أبطال أوروبا بـ(15) هدفا، إضافة إلى تتويجه بجائزة هداف كأس العالم 2026 برصيد (10) أهداف، جعلته الهداف التاريخي للمونديال بـ22 هدفا، لكنه لم يتوج بأي لقب جماعي مع ريال مدريد. اقرأ أيضا: احتجزته الجزائر ويدعمه زيدان.. من هو كريستوف جليز الذي تضامنت معه الكرة الذهبية؟

items.summary: "التورنيدو" يعود لتحطيم الأرقام القياسية
items.body: "التورنيدو" يعود لتحطيم الأرقام القياسية اقترب سالم الدوسري، قائد الهلال، من دخول التاريخ في بطولة دوري أبطال آسيا، بعد الهدف الذي سجله في شباك الشمال القطري. وخسرالهلال أمام الشمال بنتيجة 1-3، خلال المباراة التي جمعت بينهما، مساء الثلاثاء، على ملعب البيت بالخور، في الجولة الثالثة من مرحلة الدوري بالبطولة الآسيوية. وفي الدقيقة 32 من عمر المباراة، افتتح سالم الدوسري التسجيل لفريق الهلال ، بعدما مرر له الظهير الفرنسي ثيو هيرنانديز كرة أرضية أمام المرمى الخالي من حارسه. وبحسب صحيفة "الرياضية" السعودية ، فقد اقترب "التورنيدو" من أن يكون وصيف هدافي بطولة دوري أبطال آسيا، منذ استحداث شكلها الجديد في عام 2003. ناقش الموضوعات والأخبار بشكل أعمق في منتديات كووورة ووصل الدوسري إلى الهدف رقم 36 في تاريخ مشاركاته بالبطولة الآسيوية، ليكون على بعد هدف واحد خلف الكوري الجنوبي المعتزل دونج جوك لي، وصيف هدافي البطولة عبر التاريخ. كما يحتاج سالم إلى 6 أهداف فقط ليكون الهداف التاريخي لبطولة دوري أبطال آسيا في شكلها الجديد، بالتساوي مع المونتينيجري ديان داميانوفيتش الذي سجل 42 هدفًا. يُذكر أن هذا الهدف هو الأول الذي يسجله سالم الدوسري في الموسم الحالي، وذلك في مشاركته الأساسية الأولى، بعدما شارك في مباراتين بدوري روشن كلاعب بديل لدقائق معدودة. تذاكر مباريات دوري روشن السعودي اشتر تذكرتك الآن!

items.summary: The PBS Nature film "Tiger Island" captures rare glimpses of tiger behavior, including a mother, father and cubs spending time together ‪—‬ a first for these usually solitary cats.
items.body: A male tiger approaches his cubs and greets them with a head-bobbing motion while their mother rests nearby. The surprising interaction, captured in the PBS Nature documentary " Tiger Island , " a two-part series that follows two big-cat families across Nepal. The footage marks the first time a tiger "family" has been documented spending time together, and it could challenge conventional assumptions about how the seemingly solitary cats behave around their young, said Dan O'Neill , a wildlife biologist and filmmaker who contributed to "Tiger Island." Previously, it was thought that tiger moms raise their cubs for up to two years without any help from the male tiger . But this may not be the norm. "It just shows that we really know nothing about them," O'Neill told Live Science. "And they're so much more complex than people realize." That's just one of the scenes in Tiger Island that challenges our understanding of the tigers' solitary nature. In another scene, a female tiger cares for another tigress's cubs. items.body: Scientists have sequenced the genomes of three Late Stone Age people who lived in Europe 30,000 years ago and discovered that they had closer biological ties than researchers previously thought. The new finding suggests that places like southwestern France may have been critical cultural hubs during the last ice age. Shortly after Neanderthals disappeared from Europe, a Stone Age culture known as the Gravettian spread across the continent. Artifacts found during archaeological excavations ‪—‬ including portable art, such as " Venus figurines " ‪—‬ have shown that the Gravettian culture lasted from about 34,000 to 25,000 years ago. But ancient DNA has been recovered from only two dozen human skeletons from the Gravettian period, so questions about these people's ancestry remain unanswered. Based on the small number of genomes from Gravettian people that were previously sequenced , experts believed that groups in Western Europe were largely separate from groups in Eastern Europe. items.title: Hepatitis B could surge, infecting millions more in childhood, under proposed CDC guidance
items.summary: A proposed shift in recommendations for hepatitis B vaccination in the U.S. could leave millions of young adults unprotected, a new modeling study suggests.
items.body: A proposed change to decades-old guidance on hepatitis B vaccination would lead to a dramatic increase in chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infections among young people, a new modeling study predicts. Previously, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommended that all newborns be vaccinated against HBV within hours of birth ‪—‬ a strategy known as "universal birth-dose vaccination." But in December 2025, the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) advised ending this recommendation, and the CDC accepted that advice . The new guidance would recommend birth doses only to babies whose mothers tested positive for HBV or whose HBV status was unknown. The guidance suggests that mothers who test negative should instead ask their doctors about whether their child needs a birth dose — an approach the CDC calls "shared clinical decision-making." The new recommendation states that babies who forgo the birth dose should be at least 2 months old before starting the HBV vaccine series. items.title: Native Hawaiians and Easter Islanders came from same 'ultravoyager' group
items.summary: Members of the same people who settled Easter Island also discovered Hawaii, a new study finds.
items.body: Native Hawaiians and Easter Islanders genetically descend from the same "ultravoyager" Polynesian group that crossed vast distances of ocean to reach these remote islands, a new study finds. Easter Island (also known as Rapa Nui) and Hawaii are part of Polynesia, a group of more than 1,000 islands spread over an area of the Pacific Ocean roughly equal to the areas of North and South America combined. Hawaii and Easter Island are the farthest of these isles from each other, at about 4,500 miles (7,200 kilometers) apart — around the distance from San Francisco to Lima, Peru. The behavior has prompted a wide range of explanations, including that it's playful , a form of revenge , a warning against getting too close to the pod, or even a type of cultural transmission , in which one orca observes another interacting with a boat and then imitates it. But Christian Frings , a cognitive psychologist who studies how humans control their actions, thinks it could be deliberate. items.summary: A hypothetical particle could have briefly held more energy than everything else in the infant universe combined, which could help explain how matter won out over antimatter.
items.body: A neglected "ghost particle" may have dominated the universe right after the Big Bang ‪—‬ changing how the cosmos expanded in its first moments and reshaping the conditions under which matter won out over antimatter, a new study suggests. In other words, it may explain why anything exists at all. The particle, a hypothetical "right-handed" neutrino, briefly could have held more energy than everything else in the infant universe combined, which would have sped up cosmic expansion and delayed key particle interactions, the study proposes. The research was published Sept. 8 in the journal Physical Review Letters . Neutrinos are ghostly particles that rarely interact with anything. A typical neutrino from the sun could pass through a slab of lead a light-year thick — about 5.9 trillion miles (9.5 trillion kilometers) — before striking a single atom. Neutrinos come in three types, or "flavors," and switch between them as they travel, making use of a subtle quantum effect that works only if they have mass. While diagnosis rates are rising, the disease is still rare among young people. In 1833, stone quarry workers discovered an ancient burial mound at Goblins' Hill near the town of Mold in Wales. At the center was a stone-lined grave that contained a fragmented skeleton and a gold , cape-like accessory that had been crushed over time. The Mold gold cape has a unique shape and style, and it is one of the finest examples of prehistoric goldwork ever found, according to the British Museum , where the artifact is on display. The cape dates to Britain's Early Bronze Age ( 2500 to 1200 B.C. ), a time that saw a metalworking revolution as artisans shifted from crafting flint tools to making weapons and jewelry out of gold, copper and bronze. items.title: Why were the Nazca Lines built?
items.summary: The Nazca Lines are sprawling geoglyphs that were constructed on Peru's ground and hillsides around 2,000 years ago. But why were they built?
items.body: The Nazca Lines are the most famous geoglyphs in the world. Dating back around 2,000 years and reaching a combined length of more than 800 miles (1,300 kilometers), they depict a variety of motifs, including humans, animals, geometric shapes, plants and flowers. These designs were constructed on the arid hills and valleys of coastal Peru by the Nazca people between 200 B.C. and A.D. 500, long before writing was used in the region. It's not clear exactly how many Nazca Lines there are, but they number in the thousands, with new geoglyphs continuing to be discovered with the help of AI . But why were the Nazca Lines built? Scientists have been debating this question since the lines were first formally investigated in the early 20th century. Although the definite answer remains unknown, experts have proposed various reasons for the famous geoglyphs. There "are many ideas out there about their function and meaning," Ana Nieves , a professor of art history at Northeastern Illinois University, told Live Science in an email. items.body: Cryptic snakes in Southeast Asia have evolved a remarkable trick for evading predators: Instead of slithering, they arch their long bodies and tumble away at high speeds. The dwarf reed snakes ( Pseudorabdion ) pull off this acrobatic feat by keeping their head in a relatively fixed position while rotating the rest of their body, according to a new study published Monday (Oct. 19) in the journal Current Biology . They found that the snakes were capable of reaching velocities of up to 12.1 feet per second (3.69 meters per second), which is much faster than they can slither (technically referred to as undulating locomotion). items.title: Will plants survive climate change? The 'Great Dying' reveals clues about their resilience.
items.summary: Plants can't easily pick up and move when environmental conditions get rough, so they've evolved strategies to weather harsh conditions in place. That could help some plants survive in the face of a warming climate.
items.body: About 251 million years ago, volcanic eruptions wiped out most life on Earth. For about a million years , the Siberian Traps in Russia spewed huge clouds of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere, leading to the most severe extinction event in our planet's history. Equatorial temperatures spiked , making much of the land too hot for life. Meanwhile, the oceans became acidic and most of the creatures in them suffocated from lack of oxygen . Known as the Permian-Triassic mass extinction or the "Great Dying," it ultimately destroyed more than 90% of ocean life and 70% of terrestrial species . However, in a corner of what is now China, a refuge of pollen-producing plants avoided that fate and created an oasis for surviving animals. Research suggests that this was not the only place where plants were able to weather catastrophic climate change during the Great Dying, and that plants may have been better able to withstand the extinction event than other organisms. items.title: Climate change is literally altering the shape of our planet
items.summary: The melting of the poles is increasingly shifting Earth's shape at a faster rate, with the planet becoming more and more round.
items.body: Climate change is making Earth progressively rounder, new research finds. The findings are a signal of human-caused climate change, however, and tracking the shape of the Earth can help reveal just how much impact people are having on its ice caps. Our planet is not a perfect sphere. Because of its rotation, it is a bit flatter at the poles and bulges in the middle. But the new study reveals that Earth is getting rounder at an accelerated rate, largely due to shifts caused by the melting polar ice caps. This finding applies only to the solid parts of the planet; the ocean continues to bulge outward at the equator. The study, published Sept. 9 in the journal JGR Solid Earth , used direct measurements from the global navigation satellite system (GNSS) to track the planet's shape-shifting over time. This system provides direct measurements, but there are limits in how it can be used. For example, there are few GNSS stations near the North and South poles and few in remote oceans because they must be deployed on buoys. items.title: Surprising new pattern of groundwater loss may signal a turning point for the Colorado River Basin
items.summary: During an intense drought from 2020 to 2022, the Upper Colorado River Basin lost far more groundwater than the Lower Basin did, despite having much higher natural recharge.
items.body: Western states that were thought to be resistant to prolonged drought may be more vulnerable than scientists previously believed, a new analysis of groundwater reserves in the Colorado River Basin finds. Researchers revealed the four states that together make up the Upper Basin — Colorado, New Mexico, Utah and Wyoming — lost almost twice as much groundwater as the Lower Basin did during an intense drought in the southwestern U.S. between 2020 and 2022. The finding was unexpected and might signal a turning point for the region, because the Upper Basin has long been seen as more resilient to dry spells than the Lower Basin, said Esther Oyedele , a doctoral student in geosciences at Virginia Tech and the study's first author. "The Upper Colorado River Basin has historically been considered more resilient because it receives more precipitation, particularly snowfall in the Rocky Mountains," Oyedele told Live Science in an email. "I think the important takeaway is that we should not assume that the Upper Basin will remain relatively resilient simply because it has historically received more precipitation and snowmelt." items.title: James Webb telescope discovers surprising trove of metals around the Milky Way's supermassive black hole
items.summary: New observations from the James Webb Space Telescope reveal a concentration of heavy metals near the Milky Way's central black hole. The discovery deepens a mystery about why our galaxy's black hole behaves the way it does.
items.body: The Milky Way's supermassive black hole is surrounded by a surprising trove of heavy metals, according to new observations by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). The metals may offer new clues about how Earth got its share of heavy elements — but it could also make one of the greatest mysteries about our local black hole even harder to solve. In astronomy , metals refer to any element heavier than hydrogen or helium, with common examples including oxygen, carbon, iron or gold. These elements are forged through nuclear fusion in the hearts of stars that are reaching the ends of their lives, before being sprayed into space and incorporated into new generations of stars. Scientists say the material spotted by JWST likely came from supernovas ‪—‬ stellar explosions that blasted the metal into the region around Sagittarius A (Sgr A*), the monster black hole in the middle of our galaxy. The metals, detected as gas, appear to have the same composition as several nearby stars, which suggests both the stars and the gas originated at the same time. items.title: Extremely rare Viking Age coin from the reign of 'Olaf the Holy' may have been 'held in the king's own hand'
items.summary: A massive Viking Age hoard that was discovered in Norway contains a rare silver coin featuring "Olaf the Holy," one of the country's first Christian kings.
items.body: A rare silver coin minted during the reign of a famous Viking king has been discovered in a massive hoard in Norway that now comprises 5,500 coins and counting. The coin is inscribed with the name of the Norwegian king Olaf Haraldsson, who ruled from 1015 to 1028 and, as St. Olaf or "Olaf the Holy," is considered the national saint of Norway. Fewer than 20 coins minted during Olaf's reign have ever been discovered, and the newfound coin is a "national treasure," according to a statement from the University of Oslo's Museum of Cultural History. "Here we have a coin bearing the king's portrait and a cross, with another cross on the reverse," University of Oslo coin expert Svein Gullbekk said in the statement. "It is a Christianisation coin on a grand scale." Olaf is credited with establishing Christianity in Norway — an early step toward its full conversion about a generation later. "We can see how King Olaf used coinage to legitimise the new faith and to establish himself as a Christian king of European standing," Gullbekk said. "This is branding." items.title: 'The Russians were the problem in the end': Sailor Matt Rutherford on being intercepted by the FSB while attempting to circumnavigate the Arctic Ocean solo
items.summary: Live Science spoke with Matt Rutherford, a sailor and founder of the environmental nonprofit Ocean Research Project, about his attempt to circumnavigate the Arctic Ocean and why he'll have to try again next year.
items.body: Sailor Matt Rutherford has dreamed for several years of becoming the first person to circumnavigate the Arctic Ocean solo, nonstop and unassisted. He finally set out from western Greenland on June 25 to achieve this goal, but threatening encounters with Russia's security agency less than two months later forced him to reverse course. Rutherford is the founder and executive director of the nonprofit environmental organization Ocean Research Project , which gathers and analyzes marine data from a sailboat. His route took him around the southern tip of Greenland, through the Denmark Strait and into the Greenland Sea. From there, he sailed through the Norwegian and Barents seas, and reached Russia's Novaya Zemlya archipelago in mid-August. He was planning to continue to Canada and end his journey where it started, but Russian officials halted him in his tracks and ordered him to turn around. On his way home, Rutherford told Live Science about his adventures and why he wants to complete this loop. items.title: Lightest known pair of neutron stars proves Einstein right yet again
items.summary: Einstein's theory of relativity just got put to the test by the lightest binary neutron star system ever discovered.
items.body: Astronomers have discovered the lightest known pair of neutron stars — two ultradense stellar remnants that circle each other every 2 hours, 22 minutes, veering toward an inevitable collision about 82 million years from now. By timing radio pulses from one of the stars, the researchers detected three subtle effects predicted by Albert Einstein 's general theory of relativity and found that the theory describes the pair's motion to within about 1% — proving the visionary physicist right yet again . The researchers published their findings Sept. 15 in the journal Physical Review Letters . Neutron stars are the collapsed cores of massive stars that exploded as supernovas. Each packs more mass than the sun into a ball roughly 12 miles (20 kilometers) in diameter. Some, called pulsars, spin rapidly and sweep beams of radio waves across the sky like cosmic lighthouses. Their rotation is so steady that their pulses work as extraordinarily precise clocks. Very few pulsars orbit another neutron star. The headaches would occur approximately two to three times per month, starting in the late afternoon and lasting up to three days. Sleep did not improve his symptoms. The pain was typically greater on the right side of his head, but he would often feel pain on the left side as well. The pilot also reported that just before a headache, he would experience a "sense of lousiness," his doctors wrote in a report of the case . Sometimes, the pain was so intense that the man was unable to take part in scheduled flights. If he flew anyway during an episode, his headache would be even worse the next day. items.body: In the late 1800s, Westminster Abbey clergy stumbled upon a mysterious sarcophagus. The lid was decorated with an 11th-century Anglo-Saxon cross, but the base had a fourth-century Roman funeral inscription. For nearly 150 years, the tomb has baffled experts, but the abbey's consulting archaeologist may have finally figured out who was buried there, according to a new study. Westminster's chief mason unearthed the stone sarcophagus in 1869, but when experts investigated it, they discovered that the burial had been looted earlier that century. Experts also noticed that the carved decoration on the side of the sarcophagus was stylistically Roman , with a Latin inscription that can be translated as "To the memory of Valerius Amandinus. Valerius Superventor and Marcellus made this for their father." But an enormous medieval cross had been carved into the lid of the sarcophagus, suggesting that the tomb had been reused to bury an important religious figure hundreds of years later. items.title: Could 'body clocks' play a role in depression? Study proposes a new 'circadian' subtype
items.summary: Researchers propose a new subtype of depression linked to body-clock patterns.
items.body: Some people with depression sleep far more than average, wake up exhausted, habitually stay up late, and experience mood shifts with the seasons. A new study suggests that these symptoms may cluster in a distinct subtype of depression that's tied to the body's internal clock. While research has long linked a scrambled circadian rhythm to a risk of mood disorders, neuroscientists are now proposing that these disruptions define a specific form of depression that they call "circadian depression." First conceptualized in 2021 , the body-clock subtype may affect about 1 in 4 people with severe, recurrent or persistent depression, the researchers estimate. In their new study, published Wednesday (Oct. 21) in The British Journal of Psychiatry , the team identified the subtype in about 2,600 people out of over 11,000 evaluated. "Circadian depression is a biologically informed subtype," said study co-author Emiliana Tonini , a neuroscientist at the University of Sydney. "Unlike subtypes defined mainly by symptoms, the core feature here is a disturbed circadian system, which common antidepressants may not fully address," Tonini told Live Science in an email. items.summary: The fault that triggered a massive earthquake in Myanmar last year is tilted much like California's San Andreas, which can influence how much shaking takes place and where.
items.body: Last year's massive earthquake in Myanmar could help researchers better predict where the worst shaking will be if the "Big One" hits the San Andreas Fault in California. The magnitude 7.7 quake hit on March 28, 2025, near the city of Mandalay and shook buildings as far away as Bangkok, 830 miles (1,330 kilometers) away. The death toll was at least 3,700 people . New research that used detailed satellite data and a one-of-a-kind video of the ground rupturing reveals that the fault had a twisty, almost helical shape, which affected the shaking. The Sagaing Fault in Myanmar that triggered the quake is analogous to many strike-slip faults worldwide that threaten population centers, said Alice-Agnes Gabriel , a geophysicist at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography at the University of California, San Diego and co-author of the new research, which was published Oct. 14 in the journal Nature Communications . This includes California's San Andreas Fault, which is similarly tilted and likely capable of generating a 7.8 magnitude earthquake . But now experts think they've worked out why it's so hard to crack: It was bound incorrectly in the 15th century, meaning the pages are out of order. The new linguistic analysis of the document has moved researchers closer to figuring out what the text was all about. Delusions are false beliefs that are very difficult to shake; for example, a person might believe they are being stalked when they aren't or think that a major disaster is about to occur without any evidence to suggest so. In the trial, researchers found that a 10-minute session of the ultrasound treatment reduced the severity of delusions for at least a week in patients with schizophrenia or a related disorder. items.body: One of the best fall meteor showers peaks this week, when pieces of the famous Halley's Comet streak across Earth's atmosphere as fast-moving "shooting stars." The Orionid meteor shower will peak overnight Wednesday (Oct. 21) through Thursday (Oct. 22), potentially producing around 20 meteors per hour under a dark sky, according to Time and Date . The Orionids are caused when Earth passes through the debris left by Halley's Comet, which last passed through the inner solar system in 1986 and will return in 2061 . Halley's Comet is presently beyond the orbit of Neptune, according to The Planets Today , but it doesn't need to be close to Earth to cause "shooting stars." Every time the comet travels through the inner solar system, heat from the sun causes it to shed dust and rocky particles along its orbital path. Earth's own orbit takes the comet through streams of that ancient debris several times a year, with the particles vaporizing as they slam into our planet's atmosphere. items.title: بعد استئصال ورم من الرئة.. الفاتيكان يكشف حالة البابا

items.title: من أحياء أوغندا الفقيرة إلى العالمية.. قصة "غيتو كيدز"

items.title: بندقية داخل حقيبة غيتار.. تلميذ يطلق النار داخل مدرسة فرنسية
